title: Week 3: Dynamic programming and temporal-difference learning
text: Policy iteration ( rl/dp.py ). 1. Policy evaluation: compute v pi exactly with (I - gamma P pi) -1 r pi . 2. Policy improvement: pi'(s) = argmax a big[r(s,a) + gamma sum s' p(s' mid s,a) ,v pi(s')big] . 3. Repeat until the policy stops changing. Policy improvement theorem. If q pi(s, pi'(s)) ge v pi(s) for all s , then v pi' ge v pi . The greedy policy satisfies this by construction. A finite MDP has finitely many deterministic policies, so policy iteration terminates at pi . Value iteration ( rl/tabular.py ). Apply the Bellman optimality operator directly: v k+1 (s) = max a sum s' p(s' mid s,a) ,[r + gamma v k(s')] . Each sweep is cheap, but convergence is only geometric, at rate gamma . FrozenLake (slippery, gamma = 0.99) Policy iteration Value iteration (tol 1e-10) Max v PI − v VI Optimal success rate 4×4 3 improvement steps 571 sweeps 2.8 × 10⁻⁹ 72.9% 8×8 3 improvement steps 662 sweeps 3.1 × 10⁻⁹ 62.7% Both methods reach the same v , to numerical precision. Policy iteration takes very few (expensive) steps, while value iteration takes many cheap ones. Even the optimal policy reaches the goal only 73% of the time on the 4×4 map, because the ice is slippery: the intended move happens with probability 1/3 only. Temporal-difference learning ( rl/td.py ). Without a model, estimate v pi from experience: - Monte Carlo: V(S t) leftarrow V(S t) + alpha ,[G t - V(S t)] . The target is the full return, which is unbiased but high-variance and has to wait for the episode to end. - TD(0): V(S t) leftarrow V(S t) + alpha ,[R t+1 + gamma V(S t+1 ) - V(S t)] . It bootstraps from its own estimate: lower variance, biased early on, and it can update online. The bracket delta t = R t+1 + gamma V(S t+1 ) - V(S t) is the TD error . SARSA, Q-learning, DQN and actor-critic all minimise versions of it. Random-walk experiment (Sutton & Barto, Example 6.2; true values 1/6 … 5/6; 100 runs): Method Best alpha RMS error after 100 episodes TD(0) 0.05 0.038 Constant- alpha MC 0.02 0.077 TD(0) reaches 51% lower error than the best Monte-Carlo setting with the same data. Bootstrapping exploits the Markov structure (C's value really is the average of B's and D's), while MC treats every state's return independently. Reading: Sutton & Barto, Ch. 4–6.
